    Inter Milan U19: Team Analysis – MH

    📅 05 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • von Next Generation am 05.03.2025 in den Kategorien Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren.
    • Recent findings suggest that inter Milan’s U19 team is the only side in this season’s UEFA Youth League to have won all their matches so far, finishing the group stage of the “Youth Champions League” in first place.
    • Inter Milan generally builds up in a nominal 4-3-3 shape.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 05.03.2025 in den Kategorien Team Portraits mit 0 Kommentaren.

    Recent findings suggest that inter Milan’s U19 team is the only side in this season’s UEFA Youth League to have won all their matches so far, finishing the group stage of the “Youth Champions League” in first place. They also secured victory in the knockout playoff round and will now face Bayern Munich U19 in the Round of 16. This analysis will take a closer look at Inter Milan’s tactical structures and mechanisms under head coach Andrea Zanchetta in the Youth League while also considering possible approaches against them.

    Inter Milan generally builds up in a nominal 4-3-3 shape. A key role is played by the midfield trio, consisting of the two number eights, Topalovic and Venturini, alongside the single pivot, Mattia Zanchetta. Zanchetta frequently drops between the center-backs, taking on a key role in deep buildup, while the two eights serve as connectors and overload players in the transition from deeper buildup into more advanced areas. According to the Italian Wikipedia, head coach Andrea Zanchetta is the father of Mattia Zanchetta.

    According to recent reports, inter’s defensive structure varies depending on the opponent and pressing height. In mid-block and high-pressing phases, they defend in a narrow 4-3-2-1, a compact 4-3-3, or a 4-4-2, depending on the opposition’s structure. When defending deeper, they shift into a 4-1-4-1, with Zanchetta holding his position as the single pivot shielding the backline.

    As the central striker, either Lavelli or Spinaccè leads the line. Since both share a similar physical, robust playing style, this analysis will primarily refer to Spinaccè, who has started in recent matches. On the right wing, Pieri is a fixed starter, known for his strong 1v1 abilities. On the opposite flank, head coach Zanchetta has rotated more frequently, but he has consistently relied on technically strong, dribble-oriented wingers.

    To build up against high pressing, Inter relies on certain patterns that make it more difficult for the opponent to press successfully. A frequent observation is that the center-backs move wide while the full-backs push up along the touchline. At the same time, the single pivot Zanchetta and/or the number eight Topalovic drop deep to lure the opposition’s midfield out of the center. The longer the possession phase lasts near their own penalty area, the more likely it is that both the pivot and the number eight drop into the center-back positions. The now-vacated central space is occupied by the other number eight, Venturini, and the frequently dropping center-forward Spinaccè. When buildup occurs on the right side, Topalovic often stays on the far side to stretch the central area further. The wingers act as additional passing options by tucking into the half-spaces. From this structure, the opponent can be bypassed using vertical-layoff combinations in the half-space.

    It has been revealed that the primary goal of the buildup is often a pass to the target man Spinaccè, who either uses Venturini as a layoff option or directly switches play to the wing. By pulling apart the central space through the movements of Topalovic and Zanchetta, the goalkeeper typically initiates buildup through the wide center-backs, who frequently play a direct pass to the dropping striker via the now-open diagonal deep passing lane. Particularly noteworthy are the anticipatory movements of the layoff options in these combinations. The attacking number eight, Venturini, excels at positioning himself to receive layoffs from the back-to-goal striker Spinaccè, ensuring continuity in progression.

    If only Zanchetta drops between the center-backs to form the resulting back three, the left-sided number eight, Topalovic, and the right-sided number eight, Venturini, move into the half-spaces to receive when the center-backs are in possession. Through a vertical-layoff combination involving one of the eights, the now-advancing pivot Zanchetta, and the dropping center-forward Spinaccè, the midfield can be swiftly bypassed, allowing the ball to be switched to the wing in the opponent’s half.

    To effectively press Inter’s buildup directly, a hybrid pressing approach combining man- and space-orientation could be a viable strategy. A particularly crucial role could be assigned to the ball-far holding midfielder, who could operate positionally to close passing lanes, preventing deep balls into the target man Spinaccè while also ensuring that the central space cannot be stretched. Additionally, an aggressive step-out from a center-back would be necessary to avoid numerical inferiority in midfield. On the ball-near side, increased pressure could be applied through man-oriented marking to maximize pressing intensity.

    Through hybrid pressing, the center can be occupied, and the typical passing lane can be blocked. The downside is the numerical disadvantage on the ball-far side and the man-to-man marking on the last line.

    Recent findings suggest that even against teams that press deeper, certain patterns can be observed in Inter Milan U19’s buildup. From their usual 4-3-3 structure with a single pivot and two number eights, they transition into a three-man buildup shape against opponents using a two-striker system. To achieve this, Zanchetta drops between the center-backs, who move wider, while the full-backs push higher along the touchline. However, Zanchetta plays a flexible role, shifting between a central center-back position and his original pivot role, making himself available in midfield depending on the situation.

    This three-man buildup creates upcoming passing connections designed to pose problems for the opponent. A key role is played by Topalovic and Venturini, who drop closer to the buildup to fill the emerging gap between the midfield and the first buildup line. The buildup is primarily conducted through the half-spaces and the wide areas. The ball-near number eight moves into the half-space to overload it, while Venturini, from the right half-space, moves into an advanced position, and Topalovic, from the left half-space, stays closer to the buildup zone, occasionally even dropping into the first line. The ball-far number eight occupies the center.

    In a recent development, due to this asymmetry between the two eights, the wingers on each side have slightly different roles. On the right side, where Venturini often occupies the advanced half-space, the right winger stays wider, creating double width with the full-back. On the left side, since Topalovic supports deeper in the buildup, the left winger frequently moves into the half-space, opening the lane for the overlapping full-back on the outside.

    Additionally, Spinaccè overloads the half-space by shifting ball-near and dropping deeper. Particularly on the left side, a diagonal deep pass from the wide-positioned center-back in the back three can find either the winger or the striker in a diagonal alignment. This escadinha staggering provides multiple layoff options. The ultimate goal after playing through the half-space is to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, allowing the dribbling-strong wingers or advancing full-backs to be isolated and attack down the flank.

    Through the typical half-space overload, the wide area can be opened for a 1v1 situation involving the advancing full-back.

    The follow-up action is usually a cross into the penalty area. This is typically occupied by the aerially strong striker, the ball-far winger, and Topalovic. In the second line, Zanchetta and Venturini can win second balls.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the key aspects of Inter Milan’s game is their man-marking high press. With the exception of the match against Manchester City, coach Zanchetta’s team has consistently relied on man-marking and aggressive pressing in advanced areas. This approach frequently creates dangerous transition moments by forcing early turnovers.

    Sources indicate that while striker Spinaccè and the right winger are primarily responsible for initiating the press, Topalovic and Zanchetta operate in central areas. Zanchetta, known for his strength in duels, pushes far forward from his usual deeper pivot position to press opposing midfielders and win the ball in central areas. The offensively oriented number eight, Venturini, is deliberately kept out of direct 1v1 defensive duels in the center and instead takes responsibility for a potentially advancing full-back. On the opposite side, the opposing full-back is covered by Inter’s winger.

    Sources indicate that the pressing is almost always triggered by Spinaccè from a slightly left-sided position. He presses the goalkeeper while blocking the passing lane to the left center-back. This forces the opponent’s buildup toward the wing, where Inter engages in their man-oriented pressing. In particular, the ball-far midfielder, Topalovic, often abandons his direct man-marking after the opponent is forced to play toward the far-side wing. Instead, he drops back toward the defensive line to create numerical superiority and ensure that the center-backs can step out aggressively without leaving gaps in the last line.

    A possible solution against this man-marking press could involve putting the opposing center-backs in a dilemma. By having the strikers drop deep, they could force the center-backs to abandon their cover in the last line. Since Inter Milan’s full-backs are less dominant in defensive 1v1 situations, wingers making deep diagonal runs into the vacated spaces could create a favorable scenario. Once the press is triggered, these wingers should be played into 1v1 situations through deep passes. This either forces the physically strong center-backs out of the last line or creates a numerical superiority in midfield that can be exploited.

    Another possible approach could involve a high-positioned, inverted left-back. By dropping into the space between the opponent’s forward and midfield lines, he could create a central 1v1 against Venturini, who is not as defensively strong.

    Depending on the opponent, Inter may drop slightly deeper and defend in a 4-3-3 or 4-4-2 mid-block shape. This adjustment depends on the opposition’s buildup structure. The fundamental goal is to maintain numerical parity against the opponent’s buildup line, allowing Inter to transition into aggressive man-marking and press forward. Against a three-man buildup, they press in a 4-3-3 shape, while against a four-man buildup, they shift into a 4-4-2. A key emphasis is placed on central compactness, making it more difficult for the opponent to progress through the middle.

    Sources indicate that once the ball is shifted to one side, Inter looks to apply pressure and enforce man-marking, similar to their approach in the high press. Zanchetta frequently pushes forward aggressively on the ball-near side to put pressure on the opponent’s central midfielders and create ball-winning opportunities.

    While the full-backs also push high to apply pressure, the center-backs primarily serve as defensive cover. However, when the opposition’s strikers drop deeper, the center-backs do not follow them to avoid leaving gaps in the defensive line. Instead, Inter presses with one less player in the first line to compensate for the opponent’s numerical superiority in midfield. Even in these situations, the opponent is guided toward one side, where Inter then looks to regain possession. To execute this, the first pressing line must initially cut off the passing lane to one of the defenders, allowing the opponent to maintain more possession and reducing Inter’s ability to transition into their man-marking press.

    Sources indicate that especially in the low block, Inter Milan manages to make the field so compact that progression becomes extremely difficult. From a 4-1-4-1 structure, they compress the space just in front of their own penalty area. Zanchetta operates between the lines as a space-oriented pivot in front of the defense. When the opponent shifts play to one side, Zanchetta also moves laterally and looks to engage an opposing player.

    As the central players shift heavily toward the ball side, defensive numerical superiority is often created near the ball, allowing Inter to apply pressure. The ball-far number eight secures the central area, while the ball-far winger stays wide when the opponent maintains width on both flanks to prevent switches of play. This enables the last defensive line to shift further toward the ball side, allowing the ball-near center-back to step out aggressively while still being covered.

    Inter Milan’s U19 team manages to challenge opponents through a well-organized and versatile defensive structure. They can adapt to various pressing heights, with their difficult-to-play man-marking high press frequently creating dangerous transition moments close to the opponent’s goal.

    In possession, Inter also succeeds in reaching the opponent’s penalty area frequently through a very direct approach aimed at attacking depth. The key to this is a well-coordinated midfield and a striker who can act as a target player, holding up the ball with his back to goal. Most of Inter’s combinations are designed to create a 1v1 situation on the wing, where both the advancing full-backs and the wingers are very difficult to defend.

    #15714. Victor Wembanyama has dunked so much he hurt his hand, so he came up with a unique solution: The 'shunk'

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (524 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    Victor Wembanyama has dunked so much he hurt his hand, so he came up with a unique solution: The 'shunk'

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Remember at the end of Space Jam, when Michael Jordan rolled out himself off of the butt of a MonStar to dunk from the half-court line?
    • The San Antonio Spurs are leading the Los Angeles Clippers by 12 points with under four minutes remaining.
    • Officially, it will count as dunk No.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Remember at the end of Space Jam, when Michael Jordan rolled out himself off of the butt of a MonStar to dunk from the half-court line? Well, imagine the exact opposite of that play. Instead of an impossibly long dunk, Thursday night's NBA action gave us an impossibly short jumper.

    Let's set the stage here. The San Antonio Spurs are leading the Los Angeles Clippers by 12 points with under four minutes remaining. Victor Wembanyama is alone under the basket. He led the NBA with 71 dunks on the season to that point. Nobody else, as of the beginning of play Thursday, had reached even 50. But Wembanyama does not take this opportunity to slam down dunk No. 72, at least not intentionally. No, San Antonio's Martian with an eight-foot wingspan jumps directly in front of the basket... and flicks his wrist downward in what was seemingly a shooting motion. It swishes through the rim. Two points.

    Did Wemby just... shoot it from above the rim??? 🤯😲 pic.twitter.com/1YDxy8mwy8.

    Officially, it will count as dunk No. 72 on the season for Wembanyama. Unofficially, as coined by Spurs broadcaster Sean Elliott, it was the first "shunk" of his season. Or, well, perhaps anyone's. It takes a perfect storm of circumstances to create a shunk: an uncommonly large basketball player, a lane open enough to ensure no defensive resistance, and perhaps rarest of all, a center disinterested in dunking.

    Recent findings suggest that that begs an important question: what compelled this maneuver? Well, as is so often the case, necessity was the mother of invention.

    Wembanyama has a blister on his right hand. He doesn't know when exactly it came, but he knows where it came from. "It definitely came from dunking a lot," he told reporters after the game Thursday. The math here checks out. Wembanyama dunked 178 times in 64 games last season. That's around 2.8 dunks per game. Even if we discount the shunk, he's at 71 dunks through 16 games this season, or around 4.4.

    In a recent development, fortunately for the Spurs, Wembanyama has no aims to stop dunking, "but if I can avoid it, I would," he said after the win. The blister, according to Wembanyama, is quite painful. You'd hardly know it from watching him play. Wembanyama is averaging career-highs in points, rebounds, blocks and field goal percentage thus far this season. He is leading a 13-3 Spurs team that is tied for the NBA's best record thus far, and along with Luka Dončić, he is one of the two heavy favorites to win this season's MVP award.

    If he's looking for a fringe benefit here, the "shunk" might save him from the "run and just dunk" esque criticism that Giannis Antetokounmpo recevied during his MVP pursuits. This is genuine innovation in the short-distance conversion space. Innovation is rarely in short supply in San Antonio. Earlier this week, Wembanyama threw himself multiple passes off of the backboard in a single quarter. Every time you turn on a Spurs game, there's a real chance Wembanyama does something you've never seen before, and the shunk is no exception.

    #15713. NFL exploring possibility of implementing upcoming travel rules for international games

    NFL exploring possibility of implementing upcoming travel rules for international games

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With the NFL's uptick in international games over the last few years, there's no rule requiring a team to arrive in a foreign city by a certain date before a game, but that could change.
    • The NFL is currently exploring a newly introduced travel policy that would require each team to spend a minimum number of nights in an international city.
    • In a recent development, "Right now, we leave those football decisions on when the team arrives in the market to the club," O'Reilly remarked.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With the NFL's uptick in international games over the last few years, there's no rule requiring a team to arrive in a foreign city by a certain date before a game, but that could change. That could change soon.

    The NFL is currently exploring a newly introduced travel policy that would require each team to spend a minimum number of nights in an international city. In an interview this week with The Athletic, NFL executive VP of club business Peter O'Reilly confirmed that a change could be coming.

    In a recent development, "Right now, we leave those football decisions on when the team arrives in the market to the club," O'Reilly remarked. "It is something that we'll consider moving forward on: Do we put some minimum nights in a market in there? It's something we'll look at.".

    It's no surprise the NFL is thinking hard about this topic, especially after what happened in Week 1 during the league's first regular-season game in Australia between the 49ers and the Rams. The 49ers decided to fly out a full week before the game so they could acclimate to the 17-hour time difference. Leaving early also allowed the team to fully immerse themselves in Australian culture.

    Recent findings suggest that on the other hand, the Rams infamously didn't arrive until the last minute: They landed in Melbourne at about 7 a.m. ET on Thursday morning, leaving them less than 30 hours until their game with the 49ers kicked off.

    It has been revealed that the Rams traveled late so that their players wouldn't have to adjust to Australian time, but the plan backfired. The Rams looked slow and tired during a 27-7 loss.

    If the NFL does implement a minimum-night rule, it likely won't be anything dramatic. The rule that would make the most sense is having teams arrive at least two nights in advance. For a game in Europe, that would mean a team would have to leave Thursday night to arrive Friday.

    That exact travel plan was not only popular this year, but also successful. In fact, teams traveling to Europe went 4-0 this year when arriving on Friday. The Steelers, Texans, Colts, and Jaguars (for their first London game) all arrived Friday morning for their international game, and all four teams won. It's hard to imagine the NFL creating a rule to eliminate something that's working well for teams, so if the league implements a newly introduced travel policy, it likely won't be a massive change.

    According to recent reports, since international play started in 2007, there are only three instances of a team showing up the day before a game in a city at least five time zones away, and the Rams were involved in two of them. The Rams arrived on Saturday in London for a 35-7 blowout win over the Jaguars in 2025, which is why they likely felt good about arriving the day before the game in Australia this year. The Eagles ended up copying the Rams' strategy for their game in London this year, arriving on Saturday for their matchup against the Jags, which ended up being a dramatic 19-17 loss.

    There were a total of nine international games this year, and the final one will be played in Mexico City on Sunday night between the Vikings and the 49ers. If the NFL does implement a new travel policy, it will be interesting to see whether it includes games like this that are geographically closer to the United States. The Vikings are flying down to the game on Saturday because the flight from Minnesota to Mexico City is only about 4.5 hours and there's no time zone change, so it's not necessarily a reason to travel early (The stadium in Mexico City does have an altitude of 7,350 feet, so it could make sense to travel early to get acclimated to that, but the Vikings decided not to go that route).

    Under the current CBA, the NFL is allowed to schedule up to 10 international games for 2027, and if the league hits that number, it will certainly be interesting to see if a latest travel policy is in place for next season.

    Was it the early goal that should have put Arsenal’s rivals on red alert? No. While Ricardo Calafiori’s intervention was dramatic, it wasn’t that. Was it the seamless introduction of the new signings, then? No, it wasn’t that either, despite the excellence of Bruno Guimarães and Christos Tzolis.

    How about the emphatic scoreline – surely that was it? Again, the answer is no. Three unanswered goals against Manchester City will always grab a headline, but scorelines do not always define the nature of a performance or a team’s capabilities.

    It has been revealed that so what was it that should have those with pretensions of ripping Arsenal’s crown from their grasp shuffling uncomfortably? One word: hunger. The reason this was such an ominous afternoon for the chasing pack is the fact Mikel Arteta’s team played with intensity of a team with everything to prove.

    According to recent reports, title wins can sometimes sate ambition. Players don’t always want to climb the same mountain again, not least if reaching the peak was initially so draining, but everywhere you looked on a day when Cardiff was painted red and white was evidence that Arsenal remain ravenous for success.

    First Guimarães pounced out of the shadows to mug Jérémy Doku, leaving him in a heap. Then there was Gabriel Magalhães thundering into a befuddled Doku, celebrating in front of City’s fans as if he had scored, before Ben White flung himself in front of the Belgian, denying a clear-cut scoring opportunity.

    Industry observers note that another notable incident was Martin Odegaard, not long after he had glossed a fabulous display with a third goal, sprinting 30 yards to spook Gianluigi Donnarumma and make the Italian hurry his clearance. The victory was good, the trophy was nice, but the energy heartened Arteta more than anything.

    “They are really good examples,” Arteta stated. “The way the team tracks back is unbelievable, especially when, fitness-wise, we aren’t there yet. We had desire and composure on the ball. When you put your soul and your heart into every action, this is what happens. We want to do it again.

    It has been revealed that “The desire comes from them thinking: ‘I want to live that moment again. I want to have all the moments again and I want them to be even bigger.’ We know what it is going to take. We have never done it [retain the Premier League] at this football club. We know it will demand something special.”.

    You could flip that and say it will take something special from the chasers. George Graham and Arsène Wenger could never hold on to the biggest prize during their reigns and you must return to Herbert Chapman, in Arsenal’s thriving 1930s, to find the only manager who went back-to-back.

    Recent findings suggest that it can feel premature (and can be foolish) to go out on a limb before the first weekend, but there was just something about them that felt different. Often in the past they have been overtly tentative when playing City, but they came out of their corner this time swinging – and they landed.

    Enzo Maresca revealed afterwards that he “really didn’t like” how Arsenal had scored their first goal and that was putting it mildly, as there were 10 passes – broken only by the ball bouncing off Elliott Anderson’s shins – before Myles Lewis-Skelly ushered Calafiori into wreak havoc.

    You had to go back to 1968, when City played West Brom, to find the last first-minute goal – City’s Bobby Owen was the scorer that day – and how Calafiori enjoyed it, shaking his fist in delight as Arsenal’s noisy fans reminded everyone of their status.

    Latest Update: Lions' Jahmyr Gibbs laying early foundation for one of the best running back careers ever

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • For the first three years of his NFL career, Detroit Lions three-time Pro Bowl running back Jahmyr Gibbs was known as part of one of the NFL's best running back tandems, the "Sonic" in the Lions' "Sonic and Knuckles" duo with David Montgomery.
    • It has been revealed that yes, that sounds hyperbolic, but Gibbs' production is at all-time levels through three-and-a-half seasons.
    • Just halfway through his fourth season, Gibbs passed Pro Football Hall of Famer Terrell Davis (61 touchdowns in his first four seasons) for the most touchdowns in a player's first four seasons in NFL history (62 and counting).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    For the first three years of his NFL career, Detroit Lions three-time Pro Bowl running back Jahmyr Gibbs was known as part of one of the NFL's best running back tandems, the "Sonic" in the Lions' "Sonic and Knuckles" duo with David Montgomery. Today, Gibbs is showing that, as a solo act, not only can he can be the NFL's No. 1 back, but he's also laying the early groundwork to become one of the greatest running backs of all time.

    It has been revealed that yes, that sounds hyperbolic, but Gibbs' production is at all-time levels through three-and-a-half seasons. On an international stage in Week 10, he erupted for 252 yards from scrimmage (153 rushing yards on 22 carries plus 99 yards on 7 catches), the most in a game by any player this season, and 2 rushing touchdowns in the Lions' 35-10 stomping of the New England Patriots in Munich, Germany. An outing like that reshuffles some NFL record boards.

    Just halfway through his fourth season, Gibbs passed Pro Football Hall of Famer Terrell Davis (61 touchdowns in his first four seasons) for the most touchdowns in a player's first four seasons in NFL history (62 and counting). Gibbs is also now the first player in NFL history with 1,000 rushing yards (exactly 1,000) and 350 receiving yards (384) in a player's first nine games of a season. With an NFL-best 1,384 yards from scrimmage and a league-high13 scrimmage touchdowns in nine games, Gibbs is on pace for an NFL single-season record: 2,614 yards from scrimmage, which would smash current record holder Chris Johnson's 2,509 from the 2009 season.

    In a recent development, all of those feats are jaw-dropping on their own, but together they paint an all-time picture. What is perhaps most amazing about Gibbs is how consistently excellent he is, to the point that the football world is somewhat numb to his greatness. Producing 150-plus rushing yards and a rushing touchdown in a game is outstanding. Six players have produced such a game this season, but five of the six have done so no more than twice. Then there is Gibbs, who has done so four times in Detroit's first nine games, making him just the fourth player in NFL history to do so. The other three are a who's who of Hall of Fame running backs: Jim Brown (1958, 1963), O.J. Simpson (1974, 1975) and Emmitt Smith (1995).

    According to recent reports, now, some people might feel Gibbs' historic start to his NFL career is amplified by a talent offensive ecosystem that has a five-time Pro Bowler at quarterback, Jared Goff, a four-time Pro Bowler at wide receiver (Amon-Ra St. Brown), a Pro Bowl tight end (Sam LaPorta), a four-time Pro Bowl offensive tackle (Penei Sewell), and a speedster No. 2 wide receiver (Jameson Williams). However, Gibbs and his consistent excellence power everything else in the Motor City team's offense. He ranks seventh in the league in yards before contact per rush (1.57) and eighth in yards after contact per rush (3.5) this season.

    Industry observers note that among the 27 players with at least 100 carries in 2026, Gibbs' 29.1% tackles-avoided rate is the second-best in the league, behind only Kenneth Walker III's 32.1% rate. Since Next Gen Stats began tracking explosive runs (runs of 10 or more yards) in 2016, no running back has produced more through the first 10 weeks of a season than Gibbs' 34. Prime Ezekiel Elliott in his rookie year with the Dallas Cowboys in 2016 is the closest player in this span with 29. Gibbs isn't just a cog in the Lions' machine: his juice powers the rest of the machine.

    Here's the cherry on top. Not even through his fourth NFL season, Gibbs has more games (two) with 250-plus scrimmage yards and multiple touchdowns in his 58-game career than Barry Sanders, the running back many believe is the best pure runner ever, did in his 10-season, 153-game career.

    Recent findings suggest that week 11 gives Gibbs a chance to deliver an all-time encore performance in a matchup against Pro Bowl defensive tackle Vita Vea and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the No. 1 run defense in the NFL (79.2 rushing yards per game allowed) this season. Get your popcorn ready as Gibbs continues to build a strong case for being the league's most productive running back ever.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Stay up!" The pleading voice of the Milwaukee Bucks' in-arena host was still echoing around a half-empty Fiserv Forum early on Thursday night when Damian Lillard knocked the ball away from Tyler Herro and coasted the other way for the first points of a 124-114 Portland Trail Blazers victory.
    • Bucks fans are supposed to stay standing until their team scores.
    • Recent findings suggest that lillard's return to the court where he tore his Achilles a little more than a year ago -- which came just one night after the Bucks faced Giannis Antetokounmpo for the first time -- was yet another reminder of how wrong things have gone in Milwaukee over the last few years, and the grim future the franchise faces.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    MILWAUKEE -- "Stay up! Stay up!" The pleading voice of the Milwaukee Bucks' in-arena host was still echoing around a half-empty Fiserv Forum early on Thursday night when Damian Lillard knocked the ball away from Tyler Herro and coasted the other way for the first points of a 124-114 Portland Trail Blazers victory.

    Bucks fans are supposed to stay standing until their team scores. Those who are still proud enough to show up and follow the tradition get much more time on their feet than they did when Lillard was still in a Bucks jersey. They waited nearly two minutes on Thursday, then spent the next two hours watching Lillard pour in a season-high 33 points to send the Bucks to their 12th consecutive defeat and an NBA-worst 1-15 record.

    Recent findings suggest that lillard's return to the court where he tore his Achilles a little more than a year ago -- which came just one night after the Bucks faced Giannis Antetokounmpo for the first time -- was yet another reminder of how wrong things have gone in Milwaukee over the last few years, and the grim future the franchise faces. Jrue Holiday's 22 points, seven assists and four steals on Thursday only added to the misery.

    Industry observers note that trail Blazers coach Micah Nori joked pre-game that this might be the "first and only revenge game" of Lillard's career. Afterward, Lillard, who was waived by Milwaukee mere weeks after his injury, downplayed its significance. It was just a normal game, he stated, "other than it just being the first time that I've played on the court since I got hurt.".

    Lillard's aggressiveness may have suggested otherwise, but both he and Nori attributed his approach to the Blazers being without Deni Avdija and Ja Morant. "When you're down your next two top scorers, I knew that I would need to be a little more assertive," Lillard stated.

    No one knew what to expect from the 36-year-old Lillard this season after such an extended layoff, but through 15 games he's averaging 20.9 points and 4.1 assists, and shooting 35.8% from 3-point range.

    In a recent development, "He still has the stop and go, which has made him so effective. Obviously, the jumper and his legs. I think the biggest difference would be, 18 months without playing, I don't know if you want to call it rust or timing, that's the only thing you see," Nori noted pre-game. "And it's coming back. Every single day, you can see it. But when you're playing against the best athletes in the world, the best players in the world, the best defenders in the world, it is gonna take you a little bit of time to get back up to speed. But as far as from a health standpoint, you really wouldn't know it.".

    Industry observers note that the moment Lillard's Achilles snapped 572 days ago during Game 4 of a first-round playoff series against the Indiana Pacers, everyone knew it was a turning point for the Bucks. But no one could have foreseen everything that's happened since then.

    The Bucks waived Lillard not even two months after the injury and stretched the remaining $113 million on his contract over five years in order to create the cap space to sign Myles Turner to a four-year, $107 million deal with a player option for the 2028-29 season.

    "I thought it was pretty simple. I was injured. I wasn't gonna be available to play last season, and the team was focused on bringing somebody in here that they could pair with Giannis so that they could still be a competitive team, which is the business side of it," Lillard said Thursday morning at shootaround. "I saw it for what it was, and I moved on.".

    Industry observers note that the desperate ploy to keep Antetokounmpo happy didn't work. Now, both he and Lillard are gone, while Turner is averaging just 7.1 points and six rebounds on 36.2% shooting this season and the Bucks are still paying Lillard $22,516,603 each year through 2030. If you break that figure down by game, they gave Lillard $247,592 for the trouble of beating them on Thursday while Turner sat and watched with a shoulder injury.

    Five years ago, Antetokounmpo and Holiday were carrying the Larry O'Brien trophy through the streets of Milwaukee. Three years ago, Holiday was traded for Lillard. Just over a year ago, Lillard tore his Achilles in the most recent playoff game at Fiserv Forum and was waived. Now, Antetokounmpo is leading the 9-6 Miami Heat, who sit in fourth place in the Eastern Conference, while Holiday and Lillard are together in the same backcourt for the 10-5 Trail Blazers, who occupy sixth in the Western Conference.

    Industry observers note that and the Bucks, who haven't won a playoff series since 2022 and don't own their own first-round pick until 2031, the year after they'll stop paying Lillard? They're 1-15, have the worst record in the league and are in the midst of the second-longest losing streak in franchise history. Oh, and they're also under investigation for salary cap circumvention relating to Gary Trent Jr.'s $64 million contract.

    No team has a bleaker present or future than the Bucks.

    Just how bad are the vibes in Milwaukee? Major Goolsby's, a sports bar down the street from the arena, has started running a fresh promotion on game nights: everything's free if the Bucks win.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Star Detroit Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson suffered one of the most unfortunate injuries of the NFL season when he tore his ACL while celebrating a sack of New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye early in the Lions' win over the Pats in Munich, Germany.
    • Industry observers note that hutchinson brought Maye to the ground and then jumped into the air in celebration.
    • Aidan Hutchinson suffered an injury on this play and went to the locker room.(📺 FOX) pic.twitter.com/ysx9NLmNHF.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Star Detroit Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson suffered one of the most unfortunate injuries of the NFL season when he tore his ACL while celebrating a sack of New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye early in the Lions' win over the Pats in Munich, Germany.

    Industry observers note that hutchinson brought Maye to the ground and then jumped into the air in celebration. He tore his knee when he landed.

    Aidan Hutchinson suffered an injury on this play and went to the locker room.(📺 FOX) pic.twitter.com/ysx9NLmNHF.

    Hutchinson is out for the remainder of the season, dealing a significant blow to the Lions' hopes of making a run through the playoffs. On Thursday, Hutchinson released a statement about the injury, his recovery and his future celebration intends via his Instagram account.

    It has been revealed that "I honestly can't believe it. I've jumped hundreds of times on a football field and never in a million years did I think this would happen to me," Hutchinson wrote. "But even something like this won't hold me back.".

    In the wake of the injury, New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo said that he's retiring his backflip celebration because of what happened to Hutchinson. And now, Hutchinson himself notes he won't be jumping in the air in celebration anymore, either.

    "Two things I know for sure: 1. I always come back stronger," Hutchinson said. "2. That's the last time I go airborne 😁👍".

    Hutchinson getting injured while celebrating his sack meant that he joined a sneakily extensive list of players suffering unusually-timed injuries, such as Lamarr Houston, Stephen Tulloch and Bill Gramatica, each of whom also tore their ACL while celebrating a play.

    Hutchinson's injury probably won't stop everyone in the league from celebrating in the air, but if it inspires even a few more players to stop going airborne, that'll probably be for the best.

    For what it's worth, Lions coach Dan Campbell stated that even in the wake of Hutchinson being lost for the season, he won't tell his players to stop celebrating on the field.

    According to recent reports, "I hate it. I think we all understand what it is, and let's be smart, but no, I'm not gonna say, 'Nobody celebrates anymore,'" Campbell stated on 97.1 The Ticket.

    Campbell also recalled a story from his own playing days while again stating that he won't tell players to stop celebrating their on-field accomplishments.

    According to recent reports, "No, I don't believe that. I think what happened speaks for itself," Campbell noted. "We're not talking to 8-year-olds here. And I'll give you a story. I remember one time I made a significant play, and I freaking pumped my arm up and I'm pretty sure I tore my bicep, but I didn't tell anybody. I was just excited. I just pumped my arm.

    According to recent reports, "This game is built off of emotion. And if you have to contain yourself after a play is made — I'm not talking about in the moment, in the game, because you gotta keep your head — then you're really becoming something you're not.".

    According to recent reports, campbell is a firm believer in building the personality of your team. It's clear that he doesn't want to change his team's personality — which has been built in his own image over the years — even in the wake of a devastating injury.

    #15705. Tech Report: In Kansas City, Kenneth Walker III and the run game makes the Chiefs contenders again

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1014 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: In Kansas City, Kenneth Walker III and the run game makes the Chiefs contenders again

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that over the last two years, the Kansas City Chiefs had a significant problem: they could not create massive plays.
    • Recent findings suggest that the Chiefs were once arguably the most explosive offense in the NFL.
    • Sources indicate that over the years, defenses started playing the Chiefs much differently in the latter part of the Tyreek Hill era, especially after Hill left the team.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that over the last two years, the Kansas City Chiefs had a significant problem: they could not create massive plays. In 2024 and 2025, Kansas City generated a gain of 20-plus yards on just 4.8% of its offensive plays, according to Tru Media, a rate that ranked tied for 29th in the NFL.

    Recent findings suggest that the Chiefs were once arguably the most explosive offense in the NFL. Between 2018 (Patrick Mahomes' first full season as the starter) and 2023, the Chiefs created an explosive play on 7.2% of their offensive plays, second-place and just 0.1% behind the league-leading San Francisco 49ers.

    Sources indicate that over the years, defenses started playing the Chiefs much differently in the latter part of the Tyreek Hill era, especially after Hill left the team. They prioritized shutting down explosive passing plays with two-high coverages and daring the Chiefs to march the ball downfield with short passes and runs. And for the most part, the Chiefs were able to do just that.

    Sources indicate that kansas City ranked second in the NFL in success rate (50.5%) between 2021 (Hill's final season with the Chiefs) and 2023, according to TruMedia, checking in first in passing success rate despite a lower explosive-play rate and a respectable 13th in rushing success rate. In 2024 and 2025, the Chiefs' success rate dropped to 48.5%, and they dropped to 12th in passing success rate and 14th in rushing success rate. Their inability to create explosive plays on the ground or through the air limited their ability to generate positive gains on shorter plays.

    Sources indicate that defenses were particularly unthreatened by Kansas City's ability to run the ball. With a post-injury Isaiah Pacheco and an aging Kareem Hunt in the backfield, the Chiefs simply could not create major plays on the ground, and defenses didn't much care if they wanted to plod along at around three-and-a-half yards per carry. They were, in fact, quite happy to let the Chiefs burn plays on those piddling gains, setting up Patrick Mahomes and the passing game in disadvantageous down-and-distance situations.

    It has been revealed that faced with this problem, the Chiefs finally made a significant investment in their running back room, targeting one of the NFL's most explosive backs by signing Kenneth Walker III to a three-year, $43.05 million contract in free agency. Between 2022 and 2025, Walker ranked seventh in the NFL in explosive run rate among the 34 running backs with at least 500 carries, according to TruMedia — and he was 0.3% away from third place on that list.

    In a recent development, the investment has paid off beyond the Chiefs' wildest dreams. The Chiefs have soared from dead last in the NFL in explosive run rate in 2024 and 2025 to third in 2026. Between Walker and backup Emmett Johnson, the Chiefs already have more explosive runs by running backs this season than they did in the last two years combined, according to Tru Media. Kansas City has done all that without sacrificing down-to-down efficiency, which was at least a minor concern with Walker.

    It has been revealed that the Chiefs' rate of negative-yard runs has barely moved this year, while their rates of five-plus-yard runs and explosive runs have, well, exploded. As a result, their yards-per-carry average has jumped from 31st in the league to first, and their EPA per-play average on rushing attempts has jumped from 14th in the league to first.

    And it really is largely due to the running backs. The offensive line is creating a bit more yardage before contact, according to TruMedia, but the differential pales in comparison to the difference in yards after contact, and especially in avoided tackle rate.

    It has been revealed that walker, in particular, is seemingly able to generate explosive runs out of thin air. He can do it by getting skinny in the hole and then bursting through for a massive gain. He's not necessarily known for this, but it shows up all over his tape.

    He can do it by pressing the hole and then, when he sees nothing available in the designed gap, bouncing it to the outside and beating oncoming defenders—whether they be linebackers or defensive backs—to the corner and scooting right past them to the end zone. How many times have we seen him do something like this this year?

    Sources indicate that both he and Johnson can spot the cutback lanes when the front side gets clogged up. They have the vision, and especially the quickness, to make a hard stop and cut, or jump from one hole to the next and beat defenders to the spot. We've seen this repeatedly throughout the season.

    It has been revealed that johnson is also just extremely slippery. You can't get him down with the first tackler. He just shakes the guy in front of him, whether with a juke, a cut, a shrug-off, or something else. And then he makes the second and third guy work to bring him down to the ground as well.

    It has been revealed that and of course, Walker can put all of those things together on one run. He'll bounce it to the outside, shake off a tackler, cut back, break another tackle, and then keep gaining yards. Some of the moves he strings together are almost comical.

    These two backs creating yardage on their own have been a massive boon to Kansas City's offense. The Chiefs were 11th in EPA per play across the 2024 and 2025 seasons, and they're fifth so far this year. They're fifth in success rate and first in yards per play, as well.

    And that's all true despite the fact that they have been without their starting left tackle all season, have benched one of their guards for disciplinary reasons in two different games, and failed to add any talent to the pass-catching corps until they traded for Josh Downs last week. It's been almost entirely about the run game, and specifically about the guys running the ball.

    #15704. The wistful romanticism of ÍA, the club that once ruled Iceland against the odds

    📅 23 Jan 2022 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3683 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Thesefootballtimes ↗ Open Full Page

    The wistful romanticism of ÍA, the club that once ruled Iceland against the odds

    📅 23 Jan 2022 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that A little over 30 miles to the north of Reykjavik resides the small port town of Akranes on Iceland’s west coast.
    • Industry observers note that like many coastal settlements in Iceland, Akranes is noted for its thriving fishing industry, and its deep, still harbour is home to a flotilla of trawlers that combs these teeming waters each summer.
    • Sources indicate that those who do not take to the waves in search of fish prefer to take to the football field in search of a more prestigious catch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A little over 30 miles to the north of Reykjavik resides the small port town of Akranes on Iceland’s west coast. Even for Iceland, this is not a huge place. With its buildings gathered on a thin sliver of a peninsula that extends furtively into the ocean, it is home to a mere 8,000 inhabitants.

    Industry observers note that like many coastal settlements in Iceland, Akranes is noted for its thriving fishing industry, and its deep, still harbour is home to a flotilla of trawlers that combs these teeming waters each summer. But there is another reason that Akranes is a name familiar to many Icelanders, and it has nothing to do with trawlermen.

    Sources indicate that those who do not take to the waves in search of fish prefer to take to the football field in search of a more prestigious catch. The town’s resident football team, Íþróttabandalag Akraness, more commonly referred to by their initials ÍA, are one of Iceland’s most successful clubs. It is a remarkable feat given that for much of its 75-year existence, the club has been bound by its rural location and small population.

    The roots of this success were planted deep in the earth of the 20th century when in 1951 ÍA became the first club outside of Reykjavik to secure the Úrvalsdeild karla title – literally, the Men’s Select Division. For the first 39 years of the league’s existence, the Reykjavik clubs of Knattspyrnufélag Reykjavíkur (KR), Valur, Vikingur and Knattspyrnufélagið Fram had exerted an unshakeable oligopoly over Iceland’s elite football division.

    But throughout the latter half of the century, as the league moved beyond a single-round to a double-round format, the inhabitants of this small fishing town became famed for their excellence on the football pitch. Between 1951 and 1990, no club was as successful in Iceland as ÍA, and much of this domestic dominance was attributed to the labours of Ríkharður Jonsson, who acted as long-time player-manager.

    In a recent development, sadly, he passed away in 2017, but These Football Times was privileged enough to speak with his daughter, Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir, with help from his grandson, Ríkharður Árnason. Sigrún has been attending ÍA matches her entire life and is as fervent a Skagamenn supporter as they come. “You don’t want to sit next to me at a game,” she says drily. “I am the loudest woman in Iceland when it comes to the football!” Meanwhile, her son shares his first name with the legendary figure of his grandfather and is head of social media at the club. Few, if any, can claim a richer heritage with this unique football club.

    According to recent reports, their past and their future are incorrigibly entwined with that of Íþróttabandalag Akraness, and it is in their past that this tale begins. In 1990, to be precise, whereupon ÍA had suffered relegation for only the second time in their history. Though they had won the league twice and the Icelandic Cup four times throughout the 1980s, by the turn of the decade the club had somehow contrived to slip through the dreaded trapdoor into the First League.

    “You know how football is,” Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir says with a wry smile when asked to explain what went wrong for the then-12-time champions. “Sometimes you have a good game. Sometimes you have a bad game. But the team from ’83 and ’84 were gone, and the next generation we had taking over were young – very young, indeed.”.

    The ÍA team that suffered the infamy of relegation was heavily reliant on a core of young and painfully inexperienced footballers. Several of the players who featured in every, or almost every, league game included left winger Haraldur Ingólfsson (20-years-old), midfielder/left-back Sigursteinn Gíslason (22) and future superstar striker Arnar Gunnlaugsson, who was the team’s joint top-scorer that season at the mere age of 17.

    It has been revealed that admirable though it was to entrust the fortunes of the club in the hands (and feet) of youth, the result for ÍA was painful. Playing football in the second tier for the first time since 1968, this predicament only consolidated the view in Reykjavik that Akranes was simply a town of chancers who had punched far above their weight for far too long and were now reaping what they’d sown in their foolhardy attempts to meddle with the might of the capital.

    Realising that the club had been allowed to slowly decay throughout the latter half of the 1980s, the board turned to one of its former stalwarts to invigorate an inexperienced squad in need of firm guidance. ÍA legend and all-time appearance holder, Guðjón Þórðarson, was persuaded to rejoin the club at which he had found fame in his playing days.

    One of the last relics of the 1980s golden era, since retiring in 1987 he had ventured into coaching and his innovative training methods, which placed an enormous emphasis on fitness, discipline and recovery, had seen virtual unknowns KA Akureyri crowned champions for the first time in their history by virtue of being fitter, faster and better organised than their contemporaries.

    He was a man in high demand, but with KA lacking the finances required to repeat this success in subsequent seasons, the chance of a reunion with ÍA proved too alluring to ignore. Even though it necessitated dropping down a division, he agreed to become head coach and began in earnest restoring ÍA to the Úrvalsdeild karla.

    Industry observers note that the only previous time ÍA had suffered relegation had resulted in an immediate return to the top flight, whereupon they finished second, before going one better and winning the league the following year in 1970. Accordingly, great things were expected of this dynamic side brimming with youthful vigour, and under the strict stewardship of Þórðarson, they were being moulded into a formidable outfit.

    In a recent development, serendipity deigned to alight upon ÍA who, despite playing football in the unglamorous environment of Iceland’s second division, managed to attract the services of three players patently too talented for their surroundings. First, Þórðarson – who was renowned for travelling extensively on his scholastic enterprises – spotted the hulking figure of Olafur Adolfsson in the amateur leagues of Iceland’s sparse northern marches and brought him to Akranes. At well over six feet tall and broad of shoulder and limb too, Adolfsson struck an uncompromising figure at the heart of the ÍA back line.

    Alongside this mountain of a man, Þórðarson installed Luka Kostic, a Yugoslav centre-half who is, even to this day, widely regarded as the finest foreign footballer to have ever played in Iceland, even though he was 33 at the time of his arrival. Bringing with him a wealth of expertise, he was responsible for marshalling those around him.

    According to recent reports, boasting an impregnable defence aided by the capture from bitter rivals KR of 20-year-old goalkeeper Kristján Finnbogason, ÍA made predictably short work of returning to the top flight. Across 18 second division games in 1991, the club won 14, scored 55 goals and conceded a paltry 12 in reply. Úrvalsdeild karla football ensured for the 1992 campaign, hope slunk back into Akranes. With the most innovative young manager in the country presiding over a hungry, well-drilled squad of saplings primed to flourish come spring, there was a feeling ÍA could cause an upset.

    According to recent reports, however, since Skagamenn’s last championship victory in 1984, Fram and Valur had asserted their domestic dominance. The two traditionally powerful Reykjavik clubs had won five of the previous seven titles, and on three occasions occupied first and second places in the league. Even with ÍA’s return, the title was widely expected to remain in the capital, at least for another year. From the outside, the yellow-clad upstarts from Akranes were still too inexperienced to mount a serious title challenge so soon after the turmoil of relegation and were written off by pundits, supporters and near enough anyone with even a passing interest in Icelandic football.

    However, before the season began in 1992, ÍA were to benefit from one more fortuitous occurrence, one which would have a major bearing on their fortunes for years to come, as Þórðarson convinced former player Sigurður Jónsson to make the long trip back to his hometown.

    In a recent development, only 25-years-old at the time, the prodigious midfielder had been forced to retire prematurely after suffering a back injury while playing for Arsenal in England’s old First Division but was coaxed into playing once more for the club at which he made his debut aged just 15. A veritable legend of the sport in Iceland, he was the erstwhile youngest debutant in a European game before being supplanted by a certain Martin Ødegaard some years later.

    Much to the chagrin of the Reykjavik clubs – and in particular their fierce rivals KR – ÍA furnished their return to the Úrvalsdeild karla with their 13th championship and their first in nearly a decade.

    According to recent reports, it was a momentous achievement, which Ríkharðsdóttir ascribes in part, at least, to patience. “Many of the boys who were with us when we fell down to the First League stayed with us and these young lads just got stronger and better [under Þórðarson].”.

    Inclined to set-up in a four-four-two system that harnessed a squad accustomed to gruelling training regimens, the ÍA players ran harder and for longer, were physically stronger and, as is crucial to any team with ambitions of winning a league, possessed an indomitable mental resilience in pursuit of their goals. That they could play, too, was an added benefit.

    According to recent reports, although it is not unheard of for clubs to win the title immediately after promotion, especially in the Nordic countries where the traditionally smaller leagues are somewhat renowned for producing surprise victors, seldom have many teams managed to repeat the feat. Indeed, miraculously, ÍA became the first club in the history of football to not only win the league following promotion but win it for five consecutive seasons.

    Just how could a team hailing from a town of barely 8,000 people, and who had been relegated just a year earlier, undertake a championship run the likes of which had never been witnessed in Iceland in over a century of organised sport? Not just Iceland, either, but anywhere in the entire world. At the time, no team had won five championships in a row directly after being promoted. It was an idea born from fiction; a feat literally unbelievable in its design.

    It has been revealed that ríkharðsdóttir, however, believes she has the answer. “It was the same team. All the five years. And the manager, too. In 1992, 1993, and 1996 we had the same manager [Guðjón Þórðarson].”.

    It has been revealed that this continuity undoubtedly benefited ÍA, but there was another factor at play, one which, in the long roster of champions not just in Iceland but across the continent of Europe, is unquestionably unique. Though many claim to be ‘close-knit family clubs’ nowhere is it more pertinent than in Akranes, where, it is said, “everyone is related somewhere”.

    Recent findings suggest that of ÍA’s squad, eight were sons of former players, seven were brothers, six were cousins, three were nephews and, in a testament to the longevity of this dynasty, one was even a grandson. Ríkharðsdóttir herself, being the daughter of the club’s most famous player, claims a deep affinity within this 1990s vintage side. “In that team at the beginning of the 1990s, I had four uncles. In fact, lots of good local players are in the same families here,” she explains.

    It is an entirely unique footballing dynasty; a positive myriad of interrelated riches. But clearly, as the old adage goes, there is something in the water in Akranes, for such a small town to repeatedly produce an unbroken line of talent that coaching alone cannot surely engender. Genetics play their part, and Ríkharðsdóttir explains with an air of pride the stats behind her town’s unmatched footballing pedigree. “We have had 38 players [as of 2021] that have played professionally abroad. That is 0.5 percent of the town’s current population who are or were professional footballers playing around the world.”.

    Given the small size of town, it is scarcely believable that this tiny strip of land on Iceland’s west coast has been so prolific in producing such talented footballers. Fortunately for ÍA in the 1990s, they profited from the particularly abundant vintage of 1973, which produced the likes of Arnar Gunnlaugsson, Þórður Guðjónsson and Lárus Orri Sigurðsson, all of whom were raised and nurtured in Akranes. Though they went on to enjoy careers in England’s Premier League, it was their exploits between 1992 and 1996 that earned them acclaim in their town of provenance.

    Over the course of five years, ÍA stormed to five consecutive league titles. After the first was secured on their return to the Úrvalsdeild karla by a three-point margin, a rivalry that had been put on pause during their relegation reignited. Enmity had been simmering between ÍA and KR in the years prior to 1992, and with the latter enduring a protracted silverware drought, the notion of ÍA returning to the pinnacle of Icelandic football rekindled this latent wrath.

    According to recent reports, the 1993 season, therefore, was billed as a clash between two eternal enemies, but, once again, pundits and observers alike dismissed ÍA’s chances of repeating their 1992 success. At the time in the early-90s, KR were the only club capable of paying their players anything close to what would now be regarded as a professional salary, and as such could attract the finest players to West Reykjavik. Their riches could not stop ÍA romping to a second title in two years, however.

    According to recent reports, if anything, ÍA were, to the surprise of many, merely waxing in strength. In 1992, they had amassed 40 points from 12 wins and four draws, but in 1993 they finished top of the pile with an incredulous 49 points – a full nine points clear of nearest challengers FH. Indeed, only Fram took any points whatsoever off Skagamenn that year. The rest of the league stumbled in their efforts to keep up with the early pace set by Þórðarson’s insatiable side. On no fewer than seven occasions, ÍA scored four or more goals in a single game, including an opening day 5-0 demolition of eventual runners-up FH.

    It has been revealed that þórður Guðjónsson, of the famed 1973 vintage, finished as both club and league top scorer with 19 goals, while 22-year-old winger Haraldur Ingólfsson was not far behind with 14. Moreover, that ÍA could outscore virtually anyone was daunting enough, but their resolute backline was breached only 12 times all season – and seven of those came during the two fixtures with Fram.

    Sources indicate that it was inevitable, then, that ÍA would march to a third title in a row in 1994, but not without KR attempting everything in their power to ensure otherwise. After they had finished in a lowly fifth in 1993, having been unceremoniously thumped by ÍA to the tune of five goals over two fixtures, the Reykjavik giants sought to undercut their rivals the only way they knew how: money. They lured manager Guðjón Þórðarson to the KR-völlur and secured the return of goalkeeper Kristján Finnbogason. Little did it matter, though, for Þórðarson had bred a monster even he himself could not slay, no matter the riches with which he tempered his sword.

    Recent findings suggest that KR finished fifth again, while ÍA clinched a hat-trick of championships. Not that the season was without its struggles. In the absence of Þórðarson, the board had appointed Hörður Helgason, and though he won the title, he was more alike to a custodian than manager. Compared to 1992, when Skagamenn had marched to 16 wins, they faltered to three 0-0 draws and three losses in a season which saw their goal tally plummet from 55 to 35. Mistrusted by the players, who allegedly did not approve of his outdated coaching methods, he was dismissed at the end of the year and replaced with Logi Ólafsson.

    In a recent development, þórðarson, meanwhile, attempted to navigate KR back to the summit of the Úrvalsdeild karla in 1994 and perhaps would have done so had Olafsson not reinvigorated ÍA with his arrival. Yet again, the club came perilously close to that elusive unbeaten campaign, as they registered just a single loss – ironically, to Þórðarson’s KR side, who would eventually finish a very distant second to their bitter rivals. For the fourth season in a row, an ÍA player finished as the league’s top scorer; this time, it was another member of the 1973 vintage, Arnar Gunnlaugsson, who completed the campaign with 15 goals to his name.

    In 1996, Þórðarson, whose affair with KR had come to an unsavoury end, returned to the club, looking to secure a fifth consecutive title and his third with ÍA. Astonishingly, KR were installed as the strong favourites for the title, and for once, the bookies were almost right.

    According to recent reports, for the first time in five years, Iceland witnessed an enthralling title race between two heated enemies, where over the course of 17 games, the two clubs exchanged places at the top of the table before a final-day show down at the Akranesvöllur. KR had emerged victorious in the return fixture, a 1-0 win courtesy of a 68th-minute Ríkharður Daðason goal, but the final day clash is a day Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir recalls fondly, and for more than one reason. “In 1996, in the last game we played against KR, and KR needed just a draw to win the title. But we had to win. And, oh my god, we did. Four goals against one.”.

    It has been revealed that ÍA, who had been trailing KR for much of the campaign, demonstrated the enormous mental resolve for which they had become renowned, and overhauled the leaders on the final day of the season. Knowing that a draw was all KR required, they tore into their opponents, going 2-0 up by the hour-mark before Ríkharður Daðason pulled one back to set up a nervy final twenty minutes. It is a name familiar to many in Akranes, especially Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir.

    “The scorer for the KR goal was [her son] Rikki’s uncle and namesake! For that one goal he scored that game, he won the golden boot.”.

    Unfortunately for Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir, Ríkharður Árnason and the inhabitants of Akranes, the 1996 league and cup double marked the end of a record-breaking cycle. By 1997, the yellow-and-black stranglehold on the Úrvalsdeild karla had slackened, but the relinquishing of their throne was at least a slow and reluctant process, for ÍA still managed to finish second in 1997, then third in 1998 and even reigned as champions again, albeit briefly, in 2001.

    It has been revealed that what precipitated the downfall of their monopoly was a convergence of many factors, Ríkharðsdóttir believes. “Our key players have gone away, both to play abroad and for other teams in Iceland. For me, it’s extremely difficult to watch my boys play for other teams in Iceland.”.

    This assertion harks back to the notion that football in Akranes remains very much a familial affair. Those who come through the ranks at ÍA are Skagamenn until the end of their days, even if their travels are increasingly taking them farther and farther from home.

    “It is also a question of money,” Ríkharðsdóttir continues. “The main thing today is that because we are not in European competition, we do not have enough money. Our players prefer to go abroad. One of our players is in CSKA Moscow [Arnór Sigurðsson] and one of our boys plays for Norrköping [Oliver Stefánsson].”.

    Similarly, prodigious winger Ísak Bergmann Jóhannesson, who has drawn the attention of a host of clubs across the continent, plies his trade with FC København, while Stefán Teitur Þórðarson went to Silkeborg in Denmark and Bjarki Steinn Bjarkason is enjoying Serie A football with Venezia.

    Industry observers note that unfortunately for ÍA, when the club was in its pomp in the early to mid-90s, European qualification was nowhere near as lucrative as it is today. They made fleeting appearances in the UEFA Champions League preliminary round in 1993 and the UEFA Cup first round between 1994 and 1997, but without the enormous financial rewards gleaned by the continental voyages of today’s top teams in Iceland.

    Industry observers note that as such, it has been a long 20 years since the club’s last title in 2001. An Icelandic Cup victory in 2003 and a runners-up medal in 2021 have provided scant solace for the proud people of Akranes who grow ever more restless with each barren season. This two-decade stretch marks the longest period in their history they have gone without winning the league, and in that time they have been relegated twice, albeit returning to the top flight at the first time of asking on both occasions.

    There have been no more five-in-a-row heroics, though, as an increasingly globalised world, which has seen Icelandic football broadcast to the rest of Europe for the first time in the league’s history, has led on one hand to a diaspora of Akranes’ young footballers and on the other to an influx of foreign talent to the traditionally powerful Reykjavik clubs.

    Sources indicate that silverware will return, the people of Akranes believe; after all, their town is the fastest growing settlement in all of Iceland, and therein lies a sliver of hope. Amidst the squabbling rich boys of Reykjavik, there still may be a place for the wistful romanticism of ÍA. Perhaps, in years to come, another legacy in yellow-and-black will emerge from this westerly stronghold of dynastic riches – born of fresh blood within which is carried the blueprint of that unrivalled 1990s vintage.

    With thanks to Sígrun Ríkharðsdóttir, Ríkharður Árnason, Bjarki Ármannsson and Mike Morgan.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Memphis Grizzlies pounded the Golden State Warriors on Thursday to move to 12-4 on the year.
    • And then there's been everything in between.
    • So much has happened over the first month of the season that we're going to pause for a moment, take stock of what we've seen, and hand out a few bits of early hardware.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Memphis Grizzlies pounded the Golden State Warriors on Thursday to move to 12-4 on the year. The Grizzlies were a popular pick to surprise some folks this year, but nobody saw this coming. On the other hand, Luka Dončić and Victor Wembanyama are lording over the league like castles on a hill, and that wasn't so hard to predict.

    And then there's been everything in between. All the injuries, perhaps most notably. The Raptors and Pacers entered the season being hyped as new-look contenders, but so far Tyrese Haliburton and Kawhi Leonard have combined to play six games. The Warriors went from an eight-game winning streak to the Washington Generals with one Stephen Curry abdominal tweak. The 76ers can't lose a clutch game in a maze. Paul George has been reborn in Boston. The Rockets are flying. The Heat are getting hot. The Knicks' fog is lifting. It feels like Damian Lillard never left the Blazers. This rookie class looks potentially historic.

    So much has happened over the first month of the season that we're going to pause for a moment, take stock of what we've seen, and hand out a few bits of early hardware. Who's been the MVP so far? What about the best rookie? What has been the biggest surprise? Biggest disappointment? In light of what we've seen so far, is anyone ready to change their preseason Finals pick? Our staff took a collective shot at tackling these topics below.

    Botkin: It's a two-horse race so far and nobody is going to argue much with either pick, but I'm going with Luka. I thought the Lakers would be good (their over/under 46.5 win total was way too low), but not tied-for-the-best-record-in-the-league good. Likewise, we all knew Luka would score huge, but not damn-near 40 PPG huge. Throw in north of seven assists and seven rebounds and almost two steals a night, and the numbers are simply too overwhelming to deny.

    Gonzalez: This is really tough. Luka Dončić has been playing some of the best basketball of his career, and he's a huge reason why the Lakers are down as my massive surprise over the first month of the season. But for as good as Luka has been, Wemby's two-way dominance gives him the edge here. Wembanyama had the second 50-point game of his career against the Mavs, and he's averaging a 28-point double-double on 53% shooting from the field. He's also blocking an outrageous 4.1 shots per game and averaging more than a steal per outing. There's no answer for him at either end of the floor.

    Industry observers note that kalland: Wemby's been awesome but for the first month it's gotta be Luka. He's averaging 38 points per game on 47/38/86 splits! The Lakers are 13-3 in spite of defensive concerns, and it's because Dončić is out of his mind. What's amazing is he's going to have to keep up this ridiculous pace to win MVP and for the Lakers to remain at the top of the West. I'm excited to see how long he can maintain this level.

    Recent findings suggest that maloney: I won't argue with anyone who picks Luka Dončić when he's averaging nearly 40 points per game, but I'm going with Wembanyama because of his two-way dominance. He's third in scoring, fourth in rebounding and first in blocks by a significant margin. The 1.7 blocks-per-game gap between Wembanyama (3.9) and Donovan Clingan (2.2), who sits in second, is as substantial as the gap between Clingan and Dean Wade (0.5), who ranks 102nd in the league. In 483 minutes with Wembanyama on the floor this season, the Spurs have a 98.7 defensive rating; in 290 minutes without him, they have a 123.4 defensive rating. Overall, Wembanyama has an unfathomable +41.5 net rating differential.

    Quinn: Dončić is flirting with 40 points per game. He's leading the NBA in both 3-point attempts and free throws. He's the undisputed engine of the NBA's best offense, one that dies whenever he rests. The Lakers have the NBA's best record because Luka Dončić is on their team. That's it. They're average at basically everything else: rebounding, defense, you name it. But their offense dominates because he is on their team. Victor Wembanyama has much more to work with around him. No one else is even in their galaxy, though Stephen Curry might've had a case had he stayed healthy.

    Sources indicate that salerno: I've been pleasantly surprised with the Lakers so far. The pieces are working together nicely. However, the Lakers obviously wouldn't obvousuly be this good without Dončić, who is somehow taking his game to an entirely upcoming level. He's on a mission to win MVP. He's been the best player in the league for the first month of the season. I think this will be the year he finally wins the award.

    Botkin: I actually think Darius Acuff's numbers are actually too good in the sense that voters can't fathom a rookie averaging 26 and 7 without it being some fishy gimmick. It's not a gimmick. His personality alone wins him the award. The numbers are good, too.

    In a recent development, kalland: This rookie class has lived up to the hype so far, but right now I have to give the edge to the Warriors rookie sensation. Everyone liked the Lendeborg pick for the Warriors, but no one expected this. He's come in and immediately established himself as their second-best player while doing a little bit of everything.     Quinn: Cameron Boozer is probably trending toward winning. His 3-point shooting is coming around, his interior scoring is progressing, and he does all of the little things everyone promised.     Botkin: So many good options here. Obviously the Grizzlies, who are probably the correct answer. I certainly didn't foresee Minnesota holding this tightly to the rope without Anthony Edwards. But the bottom line is this is a team that looks like it has played together for far longer than it has. The roles clarified almost immediately. Joel Embiid hasn't gotten hurt yet.     Gonzalez: There weren't many people outside of Los Angeles who predicted the Lakers would be atop the Western Conference a month into the season. While Dončić battles Victor Wembanyama for MVP frontrunner status, his Lakers are in a race with the Spurs for the top slot in the West. The former isn't much of a surprise, but the latter certainly is.

    It has been revealed that kalland: Yes, the Grizzlies have faced a very generous schedule through the first month of the season, but even with that context, no one predicted a 12-4 start with Ty Jerome hanging out among the league's leading scorers. [Stands up and repeats himself yet again] Tanking wasn't actually a problem.

    Tech Report: Puka Nacua had surgery on MCL injury, will miss 'a couple of months,' Sean McVay notes
